title.zh: 中医祛痘：从根源解决痘痘问题
title.en: TCM Acne Treatment: Solving Acne from the Root

description.zh: 了解中医对痘痘的认识，掌握内调外治的祛痘方法，从根本上解决痘痘问题
description.en: Understand TCM view on acne, master internal-external treatment methods

zh.text: 痘痘，中医称之为"粉刺"或"痤疮"，是临床极为常见的皮肤问题。《医宗金鉴·外科心法要诀》有云："此证由肺经血热而成。每发于面鼻，起碎疙瘩，形如黍屑，色赤肿痛，破出白粉汁。"可见古人早已认识到痘痘并非单纯的皮肤表面问题，而是体内脏腑功能失调的外在反映。从临床经验来看，痘痘的形成与肺热、脾胃湿热、肝郁气滞密切相关，治疗上若只靠外用药膏压制，往往治标不治本，反复发作。真正有效的祛痘思路，应当是内调体质、外治局部，标本兼治。
中医对痘痘的认识
《黄帝内经·素问》有"诸痛痒疮，皆属于心"之论，但具体到痤疮一症，后世医家逐渐认识到其病机核心在于热、湿、郁三端。我在临证中发现，虽说同是长痘，但不同患者的痘痘形态、分布部位、伴随症状各不相同，背后的证型也大相径庭。准确辨证，是有效祛痘的第一步。
肺经风热
这是临床上最常见的一种证型，尤其多见于青春期患者。《外科正宗》指出："粉刺属肺，总皆血热郁滞不散所致。"肺其华在皮毛，开窍于鼻。当肺经风热壅盛时，热邪循经上攻于面，面部气血壅滞，便化而为痘。此类痘痘多分布于面颊、额头、鼻部，色红、肿痛明显，有时伴热感。临床我常以枇杷清肺饮为基础方加减，取枇杷叶清肺降气，桑白皮泻肺行水，黄芩清热解毒，再佐以金银花、菊花清透上焦之热，往往一周左右即可见红肿消退。
脾胃湿热

这类患者的痘痘往往更"黏腻"——痘痘基底偏红，但痘粒内常有白色或黄色分泌物，触之油腻，好发于口周、下颌。《素问·至真要大论》曰："诸湿肿满，皆属于脾。"酒食不节、嗜食辛辣甘肥，损伤脾胃，运化失常，湿热内生，循阳明经上蒸于面，发为痤疮。这类患者临床常伴有口臭、大便黏滞不爽或便秘、舌苔黄腻等脾胃湿热之象。我常用的思路是清热与祛湿并举，薏米健脾渗湿、茯苓利水渗湿、黄连清热燥湿、茵陈清利湿热，同时嘱患者戒甜戒油，临床效果颇为确切。
肝郁气滞

这一证型在成年女性患者中尤为常见。《灵枢·本脏》云："志意和则精神专直，魂魄不散，悔怒不起。"肝主疏泄、喜条达，情绪不畅、工作压力大、长期熬夜，均可使肝气郁结，气滞血瘀，郁而化火，上熏于面。这类患者的痘痘常随月经周期而变化，经前加重、经后减轻，同时伴有乳房胀痛、烦躁易怒、失眠多梦等表现。临证我常用逍遥散加减以疏肝解郁、调畅气血，玫瑰花、柴胡、郁金都是遣方时常用的药物，并常嘱咐患者配合调节情志，很多时候痘痘的改善与心情的好转是同步的。
内调祛痘方法
内调是中医祛痘的根本所在。根据上述三种主要证型，我分别总结了三套行之有效的调理思路，临证时需根据患者的具体情况灵活化裁，不可拘泥于一法一方。
清肺散热
对于肺经风热所致的痘痘，核心治法在于清泻肺热、凉血散结。枇杷清肺饮是清代《医宗金鉴》中的经典名方，方中以枇杷叶为君，取其清肺降气之功；桑白皮助君药泻肺行水；黄芩、金银花、菊花等均为清透上焦热毒的良药。我在临床中还常加用白花蛇舌草、紫草等凉血解毒之品，对于红肿明显的炎性痘痘效果尤佳。需注意的是，此类药物多偏寒凉，体质虚寒者不宜长期服用。
清热祛湿
脾胃湿热型痘痘的治疗重点在于健运脾胃、清利湿热，而非一味苦寒攻伐。我常以薏米为君，取其健脾而不碍湿、渗湿而不伤正之特性；配伍茯苓健脾利湿、黄连清热燥湿、茵陈清利湿热，再佐以绿豆清热解毒。若患者大便偏干，可加决明子通腑泄热，使湿热从下焦而走。日常调理中，我常建议患者煮薏米绿豆汤代茶饮，坚持一段时间后，不仅痘痘改善，整个人的舌苔和食欲也会明显好转。
疏肝解郁
疏肝解郁型祛痘的核心在于调畅气机、解郁散火。逍遥散出自《太平惠民和剂局方》，是疏肝健脾的祖方。我在临床中常以逍遥散为基础，加玫瑰花疏肝理气、郁金行气解郁、丹参凉血活血。很多女性患者在服用一段时间后反馈说，不仅脸上的痘痘消了，连经前乳房胀痛和烦躁情绪也一并改善，这正是中医"异病同治"思想的体现——调好了肝，症状自消。
外治祛痘方法
外治法在祛痘中同样不可或缺，其优势在于直达病所、见效迅速。临床我常将内服与外治相结合，内调以治本、外用以治标，双管齐下效果最佳。
中药外敷
中药外敷是治疗痘痘最直接有效的外治法之一。金银花煎水湿敷可以清热消炎，对于红肿型痘痘有较好的消退作用；黄连研粉调水外涂，取其清热燥湿之功，特别适合脓疱型痘痘；蒲公英煮水后放凉敷面，清热解毒的同时还能帮助收敛油脂。芦荟则是极为温和的选择，《本草纲目》记载芦荟"主热风烦闷"，捣烂外敷可以消炎镇静，适合皮肤敏感的患者。需提醒的是，外敷药物也要辨证使用，热证用寒药、湿证用燥药，倘若用反了反而会加重病情。
祛痘穴位

穴位按摩或针刺也是祛痘的辅助手段。曲池穴（屈肘时肘横纹外侧端）是手阳明大肠经的合穴，擅于清热解毒，我在临床中常用此穴配合针刺用于面部痤疮的治疗；合谷穴（手背虎口处）为手阳明大肠经原穴，有清热疏风、通络止痛之功，面口疾病合谷收；肺俞穴（背部第三胸椎棘突下旁开1.5寸）可清肺散热，是调理肺经问题的要穴；大椎穴（第七颈椎棘突下凹陷中）是诸阳之会，点刺放血可清热解表。这些穴位患者平日也可自行按揉，每穴每次按压1至2分钟，以酸胀感为度，坚持按摩有助疏通面部气血。

zh.title: 清热祛痘茶
zh.instructions:
1. 所有材料洗净
2. 加水煮沸
3. 转小火煮10分钟
4. 代茶饮用
5. 每日1次
6. 清热解毒，祛痘消炎

zh.text: 祛痘饮食禁忌

饮食调控在祛痘过程中占据着举足轻重的地位。《素问·生气通天论》早就告诫："膏粱之变，足生大疔。"辛辣刺激之物如辣椒、烧烤、油炸食品，会助长体内火热之邪；甜食过多则助湿生热，促进皮脂分泌；油腻食物加重脾胃负担，助长湿热上蒸；酒精更是刺激皮肤、加重炎症的元凶。我常对患者讲：一边喝着清热的中药，一边吃着辛辣烧烤，等于一边灭火一边浇油，效果自然大打折扣。建议痘痘患者在治疗期间清淡饮食，多吃新鲜蔬菜水果，特别是冬瓜、苦瓜、黄瓜等利湿清热的食物。
祛痘生活习惯
除了药物和饮食，生活细节的调整同样不可忽视。保持面部清洁要以温和为原则，过度清洁反而破坏皮肤屏障；切忌挤压痘痘，临床上因不当挤压导致感染加重、遗留疤痕的案例比比皆是；规律作息、避免熬夜对于痘痘的调理至关重要——中医讲"人卧则血归于肝"，长期熬夜耗伤肝血，肝郁化火，痘痘自然反复难愈。适度运动有助于疏通气机、促进代谢排毒，但对于炎症明显的痘痘患者，运动后应及时清洁面部，避免汗液滞留刺激皮肤。
温馨提示：祛痘需要耐心，不可急于求成。本文所介绍的方药及方法仅供科普参考，严重痘痘建议在专业中医师辨证指导下进行综合调理，避免自行用药导致病情加重或延误治疗。

en.text: Acne, referred to as "fen ci" or "cuo chuang" in Traditional Chinese Medicine, is an extremely common dermatological condition. The Golden Mirror of Medicine records: "This condition arises from blood-heat in the lung meridian, manifesting as red, swollen papules on the face and nose, like millet grains, with pus discharge." Ancient physicians understood that acne is not merely a superficial skin issue but an external reflection of internal organ dysfunction. In my clinical experience, acne formation is closely tied to lung heat, spleen-stomach damp-heat, and liver qi stagnation. Relying solely on topical medications often treats the symptoms while missing the root cause, leading to recurrent outbreaks. An effective TCM approach requires simultaneous internal constitution regulation and external local treatment — treating both root and branch.
TCM Understanding of Acne

The Huang Di Nei Jing states that "all painful, itchy sores pertain to the heart," but later physicians recognized that acne's pathogenesis centers on three factors: heat, dampness, and stagnation. In clinical practice, I have observed that although all patients present with acne, the morphology, distribution, and accompanying symptoms differ significantly depending on the underlying pattern. Accurate pattern differentiation is the essential first step toward effective treatment.
Lung Meridian Wind-Heat

This is the most commonly encountered pattern, especially among adolescent patients. The Wai Ke Zheng Zong states: "Acne pertains to the lung, arising from blood-heat and stagnation." The lung manifests on the skin and opens into the nose. When wind-heat accumulates in the lung meridian, the pathogenic heat ascends along the meridian to the face, causing qi and blood stagnation that manifests as acne. Such lesions typically appear on the cheeks, forehead, and nose, presenting as red, swollen, and painful papules often accompanied by a sensation of heat. In clinical practice, I frequently use Pi Pa Qing Fei Yin as the base formula with modifications — loquat leaf to clear the lung and descend qi, mulberry bark to drain lung heat, scutellaria to clear heat and detoxify, and honeysuckle and chrysanthemum to clear the upper jiao. Improvement in redness and swelling is usually observable within about a week.
Spleen-Stomach Damp-Heat

Acne in this pattern tends to be more "greasy" — the base is reddish but lesions contain white or yellow exudate, feel oily to the touch, and often concentrate around the mouth and jaw. As the Su Wen states: "All dampness, swelling, and fullness pertain to the spleen." Irregular diet, excessive consumption of spicy and fatty foods, and alcohol damage the spleen and stomach, impairing their transportation and transformation functions. Damp-heat then generates internally and ascends along the Yangming meridian to manifest as acne. These patients typically present with halitosis, sticky or constipated stools, and a yellow-greasy tongue coating. My treatment strategy combines heat-clearing with dampness-resolving: coix seed to strengthen the spleen and drain dampness, poria to promote urination and resolve dampness, coptis to clear heat and dry dampness, and artemisia capillaris to clear damp-heat. I always advise these patients to reduce sugar and oil intake, and the clinical response is usually quite reliable.
Liver Qi Stagnation

This pattern is particularly prevalent among adult women. The liver governs smooth flow of qi and thrives on free expression. Emotional stress, work pressure, and chronic sleep deprivation can all cause liver qi to become constrained, leading to qi stagnation and blood stasis that transforms into heat and rises to the face. Acne in these patients often fluctuates with the menstrual cycle — worsening before menses and improving after — accompanied by breast distension, irritability, insomnia, and excessive dreaming. In clinic, I frequently prescribe modified Xiao Yao San to soothe the liver and regulate qi and blood, incorporating rose flowers, bupleurum, and curcuma. Many women report that not only does their acne improve, but premenstrual breast tenderness and mood swings also resolve — a beautiful demonstration of TCM's principle of "treating different diseases with the same method."
Internal Acne Treatment Methods

Internal regulation is the foundation of TCM acne treatment. Based on the three primary patterns above, I have developed corresponding treatment approaches. However, clinical application must be flexible and individualized — no single formula suits every patient.
Clear Lung, Dissipate Heat

For acne arising from lung meridian wind-heat, the core treatment principle is clearing lung heat and cooling blood to dissipate nodules. Pi Pa Qing Fei Yin, a classic formula from the Golden Mirror of Medicine, uses loquat leaf as the chief ingredient to clear the lung and descend rebellious qi, with mulberry bark assisting in draining lung heat. Scutellaria, honeysuckle, and chrysanthemum further clear and release upper jiao heat-toxin. In my practice, I often add oldenlandia and arnebia root to cool blood and resolve toxin, which works particularly well for inflammatory acne with pronounced redness. A word of caution: these herbs are predominantly cold-natured and should not be taken long-term by individuals with constitutional cold deficiency.
Clear Heat, Resolve Dampness

For spleen-stomach damp-heat type acne, the treatment emphasis is on fortifying the spleen and clearing damp-heat, not simply attacking with bitter-cold herbs. I typically use coix seed as the chief ingredient for its ability to strengthen the spleen without interfering with dampness resolution and to drain dampness without damaging the righteous qi. Poria strengthens the spleen and drains dampness, coptis clears heat and dries dampness, artemisia capillaris clears damp-heat, and mung bean clears heat and detoxifies. For patients with dry stool, I add cassia seed to unblock the bowels and guide damp-heat downward. I often recommend that patients prepare a daily tea of coix seed and mung bean — after consistent use, both the acne and the overall tongue coating and appetite show marked improvement.
Soothe Liver, Resolve Stagnation

For liver stagnation-type acne, the key lies in regulating qi flow and resolving constraint. Xiao Yao San, from the Tai Ping Hui Min He Ji Ju Fang, is the foundational formula for soothing the liver and strengthening the spleen. In my clinical practice, I modify Xiao Yao San by adding rose flower to soothe the liver and regulate qi, curcuma to move qi and resolve constraint, and salvia to cool blood and activate circulation. Many female patients report that after taking this formula for a period, not only does their acne subside, but premenstrual breast tenderness and irritability also improve — a classic example of TCM's principle that regulating the liver resolves multiple symptoms simultaneously.
External Acne Treatment Methods

External treatment is equally indispensable in acne management, offering the advantage of delivering medicine directly to the affected area for rapid results. In clinical practice, I always combine internal and external approaches — internal regulation to address the root, and external application to manage the manifestation — for optimal outcomes.
Herbal External Application

Herbal external application is one of the most direct and effective external treatments for acne. Honeysuckle water used as a warm compress clears heat and reduces inflammation, helping red, swollen lesions subside. Coptis powder mixed with water and applied topically clears heat and dries dampness, making it particularly suitable for pustular acne. Dandelion water, cooled and used as a facial rinse, clears heat and detoxifies while helping to control oil production. Aloe vera is an exceptionally gentle option — the Ben Cao Gang Mu records aloe as "treating heat vexation and restlessness" — and when mashed and applied externally, it soothes inflammation and calms the skin, making it ideal for patients with sensitive skin. A crucial reminder: external applications must also be chosen according to pattern differentiation — cold herbs for heat patterns, drying herbs for dampness patterns — using them incorrectly may exacerbate the condition.
Acne-Treating Acupoints

Acupoint massage or acupuncture serves as a valuable adjunct in acne treatment. Quchi (LI11), located at the lateral end of the elbow crease, is the he-sea point of the Large Intestine meridian and excels at clearing heat and detoxifying — I frequently use this point in acupuncture for facial acne. Hegu (LI4), on the dorsum of the hand between thumb and index finger, is the source point of the Large Intestine meridian, with the classic principle stating "facial and oral diseases are treated with Hegu." Feishu (BL13), located 1.5 cun lateral to the spinous process of the third thoracic vertebra, clears lung heat and is a key point for lung meridian disorders. Dazhui (GV14), below the spinous process of the seventh cervical vertebra, is the meeting point of all yang meridians — bloodletting at this point effectively clears heat and releases the exterior. Patients can also massage these points at home, pressing each for one to two minutes until a sensation of soreness and distension is felt — consistent practice helps promote facial qi and blood circulation.

en.title: Heat-Clearing Acne Tea
en.instructions:
1. Wash all ingredients
2. Boil water
3. Simmer for 10 minutes
4. Drink as tea
5. Once daily
6. Clears heat, detoxifies, treats acne

en.text: Acne Diet Restrictions

Dietary management plays an indispensable role in acne treatment. The Su Wen cautions: "Rich and fatty foods give rise to large sores." Spicy and stimulating foods such as chili, barbecue, and fried items aggravate internal fire. Excessive sugar promotes dampness and heat, stimulating sebum production. Greasy foods burden the spleen and stomach, exacerbating damp-heat rising. Alcohol directly irritates the skin and worsens inflammation. I often tell my patients: drinking heat-clearing herbal medicine while eating spicy barbecue is like pouring water on one side of a fire while adding oil to the other — the therapeutic effect will inevitably be compromised. I advise acne patients to maintain a light diet during treatment, emphasizing fresh vegetables and fruits, particularly winter melon, bitter melon, and cucumber, which help drain dampness and clear heat.
Acne Lifestyle Habits

Beyond medication and diet, attention to lifestyle details is equally important. Facial cleansing should be gentle — over-cleansing damages the skin barrier. Squeezing pimples must be avoided at all costs; clinically, I have seen countless cases where improper squeezing led to exacerbated infection and permanent scarring. Regular sleep patterns are crucial for acne management — TCM holds that "when a person lies down, blood returns to the liver," and chronic sleep deprivation depleishes liver blood, leading to liver depression transforming into fire, causing acne to recur persistently. Moderate exercise helps promote qi flow and metabolic detoxification. However, for patients with active inflammatory acne, the face should be cleaned promptly after exercise to prevent sweat retention from irritating the skin.

Note: Acne treatment requires patience. The formulas and methods described in this article are for educational reference only. Severe acne should be treated comprehensively under the guidance of a qualified TCM practitioner following proper pattern differentiation to avoid worsening from self-medication or delayed treatment.
